articles.title: 9/11 vets: Do politicians take the decision to go to war seriously?
articles.description: It is Veterans Day again, which means that, alongside the free red, white, and blue pancake specials and complimentary coffees, Americans will post tributes honoring the ultimate sacrifice of our soldiers. Just as predictably, on Memorial Day, veterans will receive well-intentioned messages thanking them for their service. Of course, Memorial Day honors those who died while serving in the U.S. military, whereas Veterans Day recognizes all who have served. This confusion is hardly something to get worked up about in itself. But it is symptomatic of something more consequential: a nation detached from its military and the wars it fights. In a sense, Americans are not wrong to conflate the two holidays. Service and sacrifice cannot be neatly separated, especially when the military has become an instrument of statecraft, diplomacy, humanitarian assistance, and lethal force whose deployment increasingly depends less on congressional authorization than on the decisions of a single president. articles.title: The biggest takeaway from trilateral is the nuclear piece
articles.description: The first trilateral meeting of Presidents Donald Trump, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin, held on November 19 in Shenzhen, was worth holding for one reason above all. The United States has a clear interest in reducing nuclear risks with both China and Russia, and the three leaders agreed to discuss how to do so . Beyond that, the summit yielded little for Washington. Xi gained the prestige of convening the three powers, while Putin gained stature on the world stage even as Russia continues its brutal war against Ukraine. The nuclear pledge deserves attention, however. Beijing has long resisted three-way arms-control negotiations, arguing that the United States and Russia should first reduce their much larger arsenals. China has discussed nuclear risks with both countries in the broader five-power process and held bilateral arms-control consultations with Washington in 2023. Beijing suspended further consultations in 2024, citing U.S. arms sales to Taiwan. What Shenzhen adds is Xi’s public commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and nonproliferation in a dedicated three-way format. That is a meaningful opening, especially since New START expired in February. However, the joint d

articles.title: A gross misreading of 'Yalta' undergirds lame critique of trilateral
articles.description: Representatives of the transatlantic establishment were quick to liken the trilateral summit in Shenzhen to the supposed Anglo-American “ betrayal ” of Poland and other Eastern European states at Yalta in February 1945. Yalta ratified — but did not create — the division of Europe into spheres of influence that later became frozen into the dividing lines of the Cold War. A less apoplectic strain of the same underlying sentiment holds that President Trump’s willingness to meet his Russian and Chinese counterparts is in itself an unnecessary concession to Russia and China that merely signals weakness and does nothing to advance U.S. interests; as if the avoidance of nuclear war with China were not a vital U.S. interest. The “Yalta 2.0” narrative is not just wrong, though it is that, too, but premised in a gross historical misreading that must be confronted lest it further pollute Western policy discourse. There has been a growing tendency since the Soviet collapse to liken Yalta and the Potsdam conference that succeeded it to a kind of modern-day Treaty of Tordesillas-- an exercise between two great powers of yore, Spain and Portugal, in divvying up distant lands . Chuck Schumer of New York blasted President Donald Trump for pursuing an insufficiently hawkish foreign policy. “Trump calls the trilateral meeting with Xi and Putin ‘historic’. articles.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). articles.title: Gout is on the rise – and excruciating. Why are sufferers still judged for it?
articles.description: About 1.6 million people in the UK have this agonising condition, but it is often viewed as a comical malady brought on by overconsumption and idleness. What can be done to end the stigma? Brett McAllister-Byrne was in his early 30s when he first noticed a sharp ache in his ankle and big toe. “I felt it the night after playing football, and I thought I must have had a knock or something,” he says. “But then it just got worse and worse.” The next morning McAllister-Byrne, an urban planner, was in too much pain to go to work. When he described the episode to his family, they suggested it might be gout. “I was like, really?” he says. “Can you get that in your 30s?” Continue reading...

articles.title: Is this Britain’s most beautiful bus journey? The Welsh service that beats the train hands down
articles.description: A new coach service between Holyhead in the north and Carmarthen in the south offers a thrilling glimpse of west Wales, from mountain peaks to pretty seafronts – and it knocks half an hour off the journey As anyone who has ever tried to catch a train from north to south Wales will know, it’s quite the adventure, and by adventure, I mean chore. You leave Wales, dip into England and then back into Wales to complete the journey. The fastest “Marches” route, which includes stops in Chester, Crewe and Shrewsbury, takes about five and a half hours and costs about £105, depending on your ticket. There are lots of reasons for this: mid-Wales has some challenging topography; the old rail networks, before the Beeching cuts, predominantly bled outwards, transporting slate, coal and steel to distant ports and markets. Last month, all that changed. Just not in the way you probably imagine. Continue reading...

articles.title: India has been named a ‘destination of the year’ for 2027 – here are insiders’ tips on travelling beyond the tropes
articles.description: As tourism booms, three experienced female travellers give their take on how to make the most of travelling here • Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The 13th-century Persian scholar Zakariyya al-Qazwini never travelled to India. But he catalogued it in his famous work The Wonders of Creation and Rarities of Existence, which drew on accounts of a distant land filled with “rarities par excellence”. For al-Qazwini, as Helen Pfeifer writes in the London Review of Books, wonder was not an emotion but an intellectual method of making sense of the world and acquiring knowledge. India has long occupied such a space in the global imagination, as a land of extraordinary riches; spirituality, customs, chaos and contradictions. This has shaped how the country is perceived from afar, but it can often flatten its complexities. Continue reading...

articles.title: Keepsake County review – eccentric stealing simulator with a social conscience
articles.description: PC; Forward Instinct This irreverent stealth game depicts Samuel’s lonely life robbing garish, midwestern abodes – it’s a Shameless way to make a living For many people, McMansions are an eyesore, but for the protagonist of Keepsake County, a renowned burglar, they are an enticing opportunity. Prowling at purple-hued dusk, this unfussy thief is just as likely to steal a half-eaten slice of pizza or a naff ceramic ornament as he is an expensive set of golf clubs. It’s a sad, desperate way to make a living, a sense compounded by what this fledgling kleptomaniac carries his loot away in: a plastic shopping bag. Countless works have taken us to breadline America, from classic novel East of Eden to acclaimed TV crime drama Mare of Easttown. But Keepsake County is no prestige examination of the economic underbelly of the US. Rather, it is a stealing simulator with eccentric Adult Swim-style art and a darkly absurdist sense of humour that is expressed in its moment-to-moment action. articles.title: Twenty years ago, the Wii and PS3 predicted the future of gaming – did they get it right?
articles.description: Both launched in 2006, with contrasting visions of gaming – one focused on accessibility, the other on technical ambition – each leaving a lasting legacy • Don’t get Pushing Buttons delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The main focus of the games industry this week is, of course, the release of Grand Theft Auto VI – a game that could define the next decade for the industry. For this week’s newsletter though, I wanted to direct your attention two decades into the past. In November 2006, two console manufacturers launched their competing – and wildly different – visions of what the future of video games would look like. Twenty years later, it’s clear that somehow they were both right. And yet, in some ways, they were both wrong. For Nintendo, the Wii was the natural extension of its famous maxim, Kareta Gijutsu no Suihei Shikō – roughly translated as lateral thinking with withered technology. Coined by the company’s legendary engineer Gunpei Yokoi, father of the Game Boy, the phrase described a philosophy in which old tech could be combined with smart ideas to provide amazing new gaming possibilities. articles.title: The Hill by Harriet Clark review – distinctive debut of growing up with a mother in prison
articles.description: This unusual portrait of a young girl whose prison visits are interweaved with her grandmother’s war-weary reminiscences rewards attention American author Harriet Clark’s first novel, partly inspired by her own life, is narrated by a girl whose mother is in prison. Suzanna is being raised by grandparents while her mother serves a life sentence for driving the getaway car for a botched bank robbery intended to fund revolutionary political activism. Although Suzanna refuses the narrative, in some ways this is a coming-of-age story, but with a protagonist whose overwhelming need is to go nowhere and change nothing. The Hill is shaped by the tension between the novel’s need for a plot and Suzanna’s rejection of her own role in the Bildungsroman. Prison visits structure Suzanna’s life, their rituals and repetitions at once marking and resisting the passage of time. At first, her grandfather drives her from their shabby urban apartment to the hilltop prison and escorts her to the entrance to the children’s centre, where on a good day the prisoners are allowed to play with their children under close surveillance. articles.title: Grand Theft Auto VI review – gaming’s most depraved world is now also its greatest love story
articles.description: With realism that defies belief, this vast game easily accommodates its trademark foulmouthed, OTT chaos – as well as new empathy for the fugitive couple at its centre Tell us: are you playing Grand Theft Auto VI? In GTA VI, Rockstar has created the most extraordinarily, indulgently detailed virtual world that we have yet seen. Reviewing it feels a bit like trying to review, say, Paris: it contains so many potential experiences that it’s hard to know where to start. If you had been spying on me playing this game over the past few weeks you may well have caught me robbing banks, shooting up a weed farm or tearing along the highway at sunset blaring Bad Bunny on the in-game radio, but you might equally have caught me doing squats at the gym, shopping, assembling a coffee table or walking along the beach eating ice-cream. There is such a multiplicity of things on offer here that it is difficult to nail down what this game definitively is. Is it an interactive crime movie? A city simulator? A driving game? A sort of absurdly expansive version of The Sims in which the people you’re dressing up and looking after just happen to be professional criminals? It will be different for everyone

articles.description: The cult film director and Moviedrome presenter answers your questions on why James Bond is anti-Russian propaganda, whether Christopher Nolan is a bore and wanting to save Hunter S Thompson Looking back, how do you regard your experience with Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas? And did you watch Terry Gilliam ’s version? AwapBamBoogers No, I didn’t watch it. I felt very sad about the whole thing because my wife and I were co-screenwriters. We went out to meet Hunter S Thompson and the poor guy was in a terrible state. He was hoovering up cocaine the whole time we were there. He had a great big TV screen, with a Post-it note saying: “Don’t watch too much TV.” We said we felt like his caseworkers, because all these guys in Hollywood like Johnny Depp were winding him up: “Dr Thompson, do something crazy, go out in the back garden and shoot a can of propane.” That’s all very well, but they were treating him like the freak in the county fairground. How many years was it after Fear and Loathing that the poor guy killed himself? He really needed an intervention. Instead, he was being encouraged by these Hollywood bastards. According to the United Nations, one of the best things people can do to reduce their personal carbon footprint is shift from a diet heavy in meat to one that is more plant-based. He is a wonderful, kind and generous man, and will be an amazing husband. However, I’ve since found out that a friend I’ve known for years has always carried a torch for me, and this knowledge has made me see him in a different light. I can’t stop thinking about him, and it’s making me question if I should marry my fiance. My friend has no idea I feel this way, and has recently got engaged, so nothing has obviously changed, apart from my feelings. Do I continue with planning my wedding and push these new feelings down, or do I tell my friend how I feel in case he still feels the same? This indecision is torturing me. Continue reading...

articles.title: Terror on Bondi Beach review – these astounding stories recreate every single second of horror
articles.description: From agonised parents trying to find their children, to the man who tackled a gunman – these gripping accounts of the 2025 Sydney attacks should never be forgotten Milo Riley-Smith’s documentary is a simple piece of diligent work. It begins by spending a short time gathering the backstories of its interviewees: how they or their parents came to Australia seeking a new life, finding it to be a welcoming place where, as one woman remembers, Jews “could have a fair go” because anyone could, whatever their ethnicity. These Jewish Australians then talk about how, after Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack on Israel and Israel’s subsequent bombardment of Gaza, they began to feel less safe. They had seen a flaring of antisemitic violence, vandalism and rhetoric; they attended the annual Hanukah festivities at Sydney’s Bondi beach with some trepidation. After an extended account of the events of 14 December 2025, the documentary’s participants comment briefly on whether enough was done by the Australian authorities to protect them. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘We’re the most arrogant of all apes!’ A delightfully mind-expanding encounter with Peter Gabriel
articles.description: From sampling to streaming, the rock legend has always been in thrall to technology – but is superintelligence a step too far? Back with an epic new album, he unpacks his remarkable ideas Peter Gabriel asks me to fetch my laptop: he wants to show me a video of himself playing a keyboard duet with a bonobo called Kanzi. In fairness, said footage is, as Gabriel suggests, “extraordinary”. Working with primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, who developed a means of communicating with bonobos involving sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard, Gabriel plays droning chords on a synthesiser while Kanzi picks out complementary notes on a piano. “Look, she likes that note, which is a ninth, and then she finds the octave,” he enthuses as the video plays. “There’s a real musicality there.” It is all deeply unlikely, but it seems the perfect illustration of how easily a conversation with Gabriel can go wildly – if fascinatingly – off-piste. I’ve only been in his company for 10 minutes, long enough to ask a solitary question about his epic new album o\i: its 13 tracks last nearly 90 minutes, the result, he suggests, of a longstanding interest in African music “which made me realise that a song

articles.title: From Germany, with love: a letter to the UK | Klaus Brinkbäumer
articles.description: As Andy Burnham pushes to reopen Brexit, Berlin won’t say it, but the truth is, we just want you back Dear British friends, Germans are not the love-letter writing kind of people. When we write a letter, a complaint is usually not far off. But we cannot complain about you. About other things, yes: transatlantic relations, or Trump, ja, ja . Or our own chancellor, who every morning talks about reforms which, by the evening, we know will never get done. But when I think about Britain I feel only one thing: longing. Klaus Brinkbäumer, a former executive editor at Der Spiegel, is an author and podcast and TV host in Germany Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The place becomes a jewellery box of glittering lights’: readers’ favourite winter city breaks in Europe
articles.description: Ice-skating, illuminated medieval buildings and seasonal treats feature in your picks of atmospheric winter cities • Tell us about a winter weekend break – the best tip wins a £200 holiday voucher In December, Antwerp is transformed into a jewellery box of glittering lights. Christmas markets throng the historic squares, and the illuminated facades of the gothic and Renaissance buildings create a magical atmosphere. At Groenplaats, we watched ice-skaters circle the statue of Rubens, while at Handschoenmarkt we listened to carols courtesy of the Singing Christmas Tree. There’s plenty to do during the daytime, too: we admired the art nouveau architecture in Zurenborg and paid homage to Bruegel’s Dull Gret at Museum Mayer van den Bergh . The famous brown cafes make the perfect place for a cosy nightcap. Emily Continue reading...

articles.title: Nasdaq erases all 2026 gains as AI sell-off dampens Anthropic’s second day of trading
articles.description: The Nasdaq lost trillions in value, with the AI startup’s IPO failing to buoy it as investors question huge sums being poured into AI buildout Who are Anthropic’s seven co-founders, now worth $180bn? As Anthropic’s stock dropped during its second day of trading, the wider stock market dipped with it. On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite erased all its gains for 2026 and closed down 5% from its value on 1 January. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and S&P 500 closed in correction territory. Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO failed to stem a global sell-off in AI-linked companies, and the tech-heavy Nasdaq erased some $4tn in market value this week, according to the Wall Street Journal. Continue reading...

articles.title: Household rush to stockpile emergency supplies sends British retail sales soaring
articles.description: Surge fuelled by ‘preppers’ heeding Be Ready campaign’s call for households to have three days of food and water for emergencies Retail sales in Great Britain surged last month as the public rushed to buy products including tinned food and long-life milk, after the government issued a warning to stock up in case of a disaster. The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said the volume of goods sold jumped by 0.7% month on month in October, defying economists’ consensus expectations of flat sales, as “preppers” took heed of the government’s Be Ready campaign to hold supplies to last 72 hours to survive a possible extreme weather event, cyber incident or another serious emergency. Continue reading...

articles.title: Ebola killed 46 members of one man’s family. Now he is fighting to save the rest
articles.description: Six months after the Bundibugyo strain swept through eastern DR Congo, Sylvain Kabona Tibasima is still trying to warn friends and family about the dangers of the virus The day Birungi Nembe was born in a hospital in Bunia, in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, her mother, Sylvie Bongerize Tibasima, 46, was diagnosed with Ebola. Sylvie died a week later, leaving behind her husband and nine children, including her newborn daughter. But the little girl had contracted the virus shortly after birth as well. Two weeks later, in early September, her tiny body was placed in a wooden coffin, which was nailed shut and lowered into a small grave by a burial worker dressed in protective gear. Few relatives attended; the risk of infection was just too high. Continue reading...

articles.title: Eat your cup: could edible packaging help solve the world’s plastic problem?
articles.description: Experts say seaweed could be a solution in the fight against global plastic waste, which doubled between 2000 and 2019 The name of the Northamptonshire hamlet of Nobottle means “new building” in Old English. But on a Tuesday last month, the name of the tiny cluster of houses in the East Midlands took on a whole different meaning. Parked on a driveway opposite the village green, a van handed out Innocent ginger shots with one notable difference: there was no bottle. The drinks were in edible pods as part of a pilot project with Notpla, a company that makes biodegradable packaging. Roughly half of the 30 or so local residents tried the product lined up on trays. Continue reading...

articles.title: Pacific islanders face a ‘sickening disconnect’ between Cop31 and the climate devastation at their doorstep
articles.description: As the UN summit nears its close, the ‘frustratingly’ slow progress and lack of focus on fossil fuel transition have the Pacific turning elsewhere for help “I need to go to sleep every night wondering what that means, you know?” says Albon Ishoda, leaning against a wall in a corridor at the UN climate summit in Turkey. “For us, it’s about existence.” Ishoda is a diplomat who works for the Marshall Islands – a group of low-lying atolls that are specks on a map in the ocean between Hawaii and Australia. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I was drinking at 15, going to parties, being groomed and abused’: the grim reality of age-gap relationships
articles.description: Do teenagers need more protection from predatory adults? As campaigners in the UK call for changes to the law on consent, we talk to five people who became entangled with much older men and women In the wake of the allegations against David Walliams (which he denies) – that he wooed young fans with promises of professional help – there have been renewed calls for a staggered age of consent. Sometimes called Romeo and Juliet laws, rules already exist in some US states, Canada and France to prevent “age-gap relationships” or, to put it another way, the sexual exploitation of teenagers by adults. The suggestion from UK campaigners Close the Consent Gap is for it to be illegal to have an age gap of more than three years if anyone is under 18, and last week, Claire Waxman, the victims’ commissioner for England and Wales, called for “serious conversations” on the potential for legislative change . I have spoken to people in their 40s, 50s, 60s and 70s, describing age gaps far greater than three years; often with people twice their age or more. It’s noticeable that social norms and taboos didn’t change hugely between the start of the 1960s and the end of the 80s; in most cases, their pare

articles.title: Pink Rabbit: the provocative bedroom drama about a Muslim OnlyFans star interrupted by her mum
articles.description: In Farah Ashraf’s solo show an obedient daughter secretly does online sex work as ‘PersianBaby’. The actor and writer explains how two worlds collide in her darkly funny play At home, Amna is the modest and dutiful Muslim daughter of her parents’ dreams. Online, armed with a webcam and an OnlyFans account, she is PersianBaby – an exoticised version of herself complete with fake accent, designed to entice men willing to part with their cash. Pink Rabbit, writer-performer Farah Ashraf’s provocative and darkly funny solo play, is a nuanced account of being caught between the private life of desire and the cultural expectations that shape how she is perceived. “I loved this idea of push and pull, and two different worlds,” says Ashraf who began work on the play during her final year at the Oxford School of Drama, before which she had trained with the National Youth Theatre. Continue reading...

articles.title: Lewis Hamilton is now the apex sports protester as US athletes stay silent
articles.description: The Ferrari driver has always used his fame to highlight causes he cares about. Now he stands out as other athletes tone down their rhetoric Most Formula One drivers might slip away to the beach or the golf course on a week off between races. Lewis Hamilton is not most drivers, though. Instead he went to the Rafah border crossing between Egypt and Gaza. He greeted aid workers in Arabic, toured the checkpoint and visited the Egyptian Red Crescent warehouses in nearby El-Arish, where relief supplies are prepared for distribution. Hamilton made the visit on a day Israeli airstrikes and gunfire killed at least seven Palestinians in Gaza, adding to a death toll that’s climbed above 74,000 since war broke out three years ago. He wore dark glasses and dressed head to toe in black. “The past three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling,” he wrote on Instagram of his visit, before turning the lens on himself. “I know so many people that feel that same helplessness. That same need to do something rather than watch. I don’t want us to get used to their suffering. I don’t want us to look away.” Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The hand of god’ and all that: Lineker, Shilton et al look back at 1986 England-Argentina clash – The Match review
articles.description: Argentinian co-directors Juan Cabral and Santiago Franco work hard to appear impartial in account that situates the game in a long continuum of conflict Here is a football documentary that is a cut above the drain-clogging content that loiters in streaming platforms everywhere. Its subject is the World Cup quarter-final contest between Argentina and England in 1986, a game constantly replayed in the collective consciousness for the two never-to-be-forgotten moments contributed by Diego Maradona: the illicit “hand of God” goal that gave Argentina the lead, and then five minutes later his sublime second goal, for which he skipped past half a dozen of the England team before slotting the ball home with the outside of his foot. It was this second strike, voted in 2002 as Fifa’s goal of the century , that partly lanced the boil of English rage over Maradona’s outrageous cheating; what could they do in the face of such authentic genius? Over and above football matters, it’s clear to see that there were bigger things at stake. Rather obviously, it happened only four years after the Falklands war, which thoroughly poisoned already tense relations between Britain and Argentina. The Match si

articles.title: I, too, was raped by my partner while drugged and unconscious. There are more survivors than you think | Zoe Watts
articles.description: Before Gisèle Pelicot and now Joanne Young, drug-facilitated rape was virtually unheard of. I now realise that my own horrific ordeal was not unique Like many, I followed closely the sickening case of Philip Young, who has been convicted of repeatedly drugging and raping his now ex-wife, Joanne Young, and advertising her on the internet for sex. It is, to any right-thinking person, unimaginably horrific that the person you’re supposed to trust most in the world would betray you in this, the worst possible way. I don’t have to imagine it, however. I have lived it. The man I had been with since I was 17 – my husband and the father of my four children, the man who had vowed to love and look after me and with whom I had shared a bed for almost 7,000 nights – did the same to me. Zoe Watts is a campaigner and cofounder of the #EndEyeCheck campaign to raise awareness of drug-facilitated sexual abuse Information and support for anyone affected by rape or sexual abuse issues is available from the following organisations. In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland , or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland . In the US, Rainn offers supp

articles.title: The UK government ridicules villages such as Piddington – but it’s these ‘Nimbys’ who show us the way | Simon Jenkins
articles.description: In other countries, local communities have a say in their futures. If the UK were truly democratic, everywhere would be a parish in control of its own fate Poor Piddington. The Oxfordshire village of just 350 people was told last week by the communities secretary, Angela Rayner, that it must almost quadruple in size. That wasn’t all. The newcomers would be 1,250 young asylum seekers, mainly from Afghanistan and Eritrea, victims of Britain’s chaotic asylum appeal system. They will be housed in former military cabins on the village’s outskirts. Rayner said that this was an “urgent crown development”, which allowed her to ignore local objections. And there had certainly been objections. In September, Piddington villagers declared they were fed up with Britain. Led by their parish council and on a 92% turnout, they voted overwhelmingly to leave the UK and become a “principality”. They are joined in their protest by Barnham in Suffolk, where locals have been told this week that they are to host nearly 1,000 asylum seekers. They have set their own date on a referendum to leave the UK. Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist, author and BBC broadcaster. His book The Village in Britain: And

articles.title: Men’s tennis boosts prize money for players to more than $350m in major overhaul
articles.description: Cash increase via ATP’s creation of ‘One Vision’ company More rest breaks added to reduce player welfare issues The Association of Tennis Professionals (ATP) has approved major changes to the financial structure of men’s tennis that will make the total prize money available to the players increase to more than $350m (£267m) by 2028, from $270m this year. The creation of a new company to sell all the tour’s media, commercial and data rights, ATP Ventures, will lead to the investment of an additional $100m in player remuneration including an increased $50m bonus pool, a $25m year-end rankings bonus and $26m player pensions. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘My body started consuming itself. I was a millimetre from death’: Andrey Zvyagintsev on Covid, Putin and life in exile
articles.description: The Russian film-maker spent 40 days in a coma and suffered 92% lung damage during the pandemic. He describes how making new movie Minotaur helped his rehabilitation Andrey Zvyagintsev tells the tale of a knight who is riding through a dark forest and sees a stone sign at a fork in the road. The sign says that if he turns left he will lose his horse and if he turns right he will lose his head. So the knight has a dilemma; there are only bad options here. Zvyagintsev smiles and says: “It is a very Russian fairytale.” Terrible things tend to happen, that’s the way the world works, and a person is defined by how they respond to each challenge. That goes for the knight in the forest and the characters in a film. It probably goes for Zvyagintsev, too, who has lost not his horse but his home and very nearly his life. The Russian director almost died during the Covid-19 pandemic and spent 40 days in an induced coma . He now lives in exile as an enemy of the state. “I’m with the birds,” he says by way of explaining his situation. “Birds have no borders. They’re not thinking about tomorrow.” Continue reading...

articles.title: The month’s best experimental album: Stella Z’s ambient adventures into lucid dreaming
articles.description: (CDR) Based around sounds recorded on her trips back to China, the Fujian-born, London-based producer creates a curious nocturnal collage on Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming Lucid dreaming is one of the influences behind Thunder Is the Sky Dreaming, the new record from Fujian-born, London-based producer Stella Z. “Every night is an adventure,” she writes in the liner notes, “I can even smell things in certain dreams.” The eight tracks here are suitably sensory, scattered with effervescent sounds, ephemeral whispers and polyrhythmic percussion. Many of the sounds and textures were recorded during trips back to China – the ambient noises of a pharmacy or the Fujian mountains late at night – a curious, collage-like approach that underpins the record. On The Somnium Is Awaiting My Cue, we hear what appear to be insects buzzing around a plodding bassline and sporadic woodwind motifs, while electronics softly spiral. Similarly hypnotic is Mira Miruna, on which the echoes of words gradually reveal themselves among the fizzing, softly discordant arrangement: a warped, increasingly urgent call to “wake up”, reminiscent of the foggy state as you rise from sleep. Z amplifies this heady feeling lat

articles.title: Take That: Dreamers review – 50-something boyband fail to relight the fire on nostalgia-drenched return
articles.description: (EMI) The pallid disco revivalism sounds like S Club 7 and the folksy stomp-clap like Mumford and Sons – yet a few standout moments prove they can still strike gold if they try Listening to Wonderkids, the string-laden opener of Take That’s new album, it seems the three remaining fiftysomething boybanders are feeling reflective. “Forgiving you, forgiving me / This vicious circle is now complete,” sings Gary Barlow. In the years since their last record, the band – and former member Robbie Williams – have indeed laid out the trials and tribulations of 35 years of Take That in several documentaries, some more candid than others. Earlier this year, they even embarked on a revival of their blockbuster 2009 Circus tour. Unfortunately, all this reminiscing has left their 10th album feeling so steeped in nostalgia that any moments of greatness struggle for attention. Continue reading...

articles.title: Green Kingdom by Ben Dark review – a luscious natural history of plant life
articles.description: A gardener traces the dynasties that dominate the vegetal world in appropriately sumptuous prose John Ruskin, the Victorian writer and critic, hated the way science insisted on turning his beloved natural world into something smutty. Botanists, he complained, used “microscopic malice” to reduce the spurs, petals and stamens of his favourite flowers to “obscene processes and prurient apparitions”. Others were less squeamish. In 1908, Marie Stopes, the scientist who later became a champion of birth control, spent three days in Japan’s Matsushima Bay in a state of “grand excitement” hunting ginkgo sperms. Oliver Sacks, the neurologist, passed his adolescence at Kew gawping at the cycads’ sexual organs. Reading Ben Dark’s excellent account, it is hard not to conclude that even the most modest plants are living in a state of permanent arousal. Each of Dark’s chapters tells the story of one plant dynasty, from rootless, seedless pond scum to alpine meadows. Some 97% of all the species that have ever existed are already extinct, but traces of them live on in their descendants, and it is these ancient threads that Dark pursues in this absorbing book. He is a professional gardener, yet his

articles.title: Jodi Picoult: ‘Reading Ta-Nehisi Coates made me rethink racism’
articles.description: The American novelist on the wild side of Maurice Sendak, re-evaluating Gone With the Wind, and the magical comforts of Alice Hoffman My favourite book growing up I loved Maurice Sendak’s Where the Wild Things Are. Max’s visit to the land of monsters is escapist, of course, but there’s darkness and poetry in it, too. “The walls became the world all around” has always stuck with me. The book that changed me as a teenager A Tree Grows in Brooklyn by Betty Smith. My mom gave it to me at around 12 or 13, and I remember thinking it was such an adult book at the time. It gave me a protagonist to admire who thrived in spite of the setbacks in her life, and also helped put into perspective the charmed life I’d been living. Continue reading...

articles.title: Steps review – Netflix’s Disney-lite Cinderella rework has enough pep in its step
articles.description: The plot might be a little overstuffed and the animation style could be a little more distinctive, but this is better than the streamer’s average animated offering Stop me if you’ve heard this one before, but that age-old story you think you know, well, you might not know it at all. It’s a tale as old as Shrek, which was by no means the first film to subvert fairytale expectations, but it was definitely the most influential, and we’re still feeling its impact 25 years later, for better or worse. What if that villain wasn’t actually the villain after all? What if that love interest shouldn’t have been of interest in the first place? What if that damsel in distress was given a bullet-speed fight scene instead of weeping in a tower? But what might have seemed fresh in 2001, if not quite as fresh for anyone who knew and loved The Princess Bride , has grown a little tiresome ever since. Bucking the conventions has essentially become the convention, and effortful attempts to remix classic storytelling beats have mostly ended up reeking of smugness. Yet they still keep coming (IP is king) and before the inevitable Shrek legacy sequel hits cinemas next summer, Netflix is trying to conjure

articles.title: Chia pudding, pickle and picky dog food: whose fridge is this?
articles.description: ‘Elbow noodles’ for a pet? Obsessed with labels, and jam-packed with condiments, it could only be author and chef Carla Lalli … Cheese I pretty much always have parm or grana padano, and pecorino, for pasta, Caesar salad or a dressing. I’ll have a parmesan rind in the mix, too, for when I’m cooking beans or grains. Then, there’s snacking cheese: sliced cheddar, Pepper Jack or muenster from the deli section for a quesadilla when Cosmo [Lalli’s son] gets home. I love mozzarella sticks for a protein snack, or sometimes when I’m alone, I’ll melt them on stir-fried rice with kimchi, or Korean rice cakes. I always have them in the summer when I go to the beach, too. Marge’s food This is my dog’s food. The usual recipe is a mix of ground minced turkey, minced beef, chicken liver, chicken gizzards, carrot, butternut squash, some frozen kale or spinach, elbow noodles and rice. I truly did not think I would ever be this person, but she’s so picky about her food … I wonder why! But I did get sick of buying food and her leaving half of it behind. Continue reading...

articles.title: Benjamina Ebuehi’s recipe for maple custard tart | The sweet spot
articles.description: Maple syrup brings woody, caramel flavours to this yummy baked custard tart I’ve been using maple syrup as a sweetener more and more, because it tastes great and can be an easy way to introduce an extra woody, caramel flavour to bakes and desserts. Its delicate flavour can sometimes get lost in heavier recipes, but in this custard tart it shines, instantly making it feel more warm and cosy. Use a darker maple syrup for a more prominent maple flavour. Continue reading...

articles.title: In a flap: how the butterfly became a symbol of gen Z resilience – and anxiety
articles.description: The delicate insect has become fashion’s favourite motif again – but having represented sexuality in the 90s and the soul in Greco-Roman times, what does it say about youth culture today? • Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here In the new Gucci campaign, Mariah Carey blows a goodbye kiss to 2026 in the most Mariahhhh way possible. Dressed in a fake fur coat and an azure dress, she enters a Christmas party to the twinkly sounds of All I Want For Christmas Is You. There are beautiful people, presents wrapped with Gucci string and butterflies, which have been associated with the popstar since her 1997 album, Butterfly, but have recently fluttered back to become a symbol of gen Z defiance and girlhood. Carey serves as fairy godmother to the other “pop girlies” who have embraced the emblem, from PinkPantheress to Dua Lipa; Rachel Chinouriri to Marina and the Diamonds. At the Academy Museum gala in October, the singer Janelle Monáe looked as if she might take flight in a Robert Wun couture gown, with wide, yonic wings. Elsewhere, Tate McRae recently wore a black sequined butterfly bra and matching butterfly wing belt from lingerie wunderkind Ludovic de Saint S

articles.title: Garden composting may not be glamorous, but it brings rich rewards
articles.description: It’s hardly the most exciting aspect of gardening, but getting stuck in now will leave you reaping the benefits in the new year I am going to do the thing that put me off every gardening book I read for the first few years of teaching myself how to garden, and smugly lecture about the importance of soil. But I thought it would be less painful in late November, that languid hinterland between the crisp crunch of bright autumn and the mania of Christmas. If you’d rather, I could bang on about tool-cleaning? Thought not. I am currently evolving into my next method of composting and getting proper compost bays. When we moved in, we inherited a couple of tall plastic bins – or “Daleks” as my fellow columnist Claire Ratinon calls them. Considering I’ve paid very little attention to the compost for the past 15 months, aside from throwing all of our raw fruit and vegetable waste in there, along with leaves and some cardboard, they’ve coped admirably. Continue reading...

articles.title: Country diary: It’s been a strange year for seasons – now our fungi are in disarray | Michael White
articles.description: Cranbrook, Kent: Some species are absent, some have appeared twice – this may be a hangover from the summer drought and ‘second spring’ As autumn intensifies, it is easy for surface-dwellers such as ourselves to forget that we have already seen the trees turn once this year – not from shortening days, but for want of water. Summer turned leaves and meadows brown, until heavy rain in September and a second “spring” painted green all signs of the drought here in Kent, and banished at a stroke our fleeting interest in it. Subterranean organisms, though, and those that span both worlds, have far longer memories. The boundary oak between the lower paddocks will now for ever have a narrow growth-ring within its girth, and fungi, to the human eye at least, have been sent into utter disarray. Continue reading...

articles.title: UK teachers: have you experienced abuse in schools?
articles.description: We’d like to hear people’s experiences of incidents of abuse while working in UK schools. Since the pandemic, many schools have reported rising pupil violence , misogynistic abuse of female staff is on the increase , and teachers have observed a rise in problem parents. We would like to hear from teachers about their experiences of seeing or being the victim of violence and abuse in schools, from either pupils or parents, within the last five years. What happened and was the incident reported? If the police were involved, what was the outcome? Please do not include any identifying details of the children involved. Continue reading...

articles.title: Andy, António and Ursula: the joyful EU throuple break Nigel’s bitter heart | John Crace
articles.description: The passionate PM was unafraid to rush in. This could be the start of something lasting … if people could conquer their trust issues Forget the smell. You could almost taste the madeleines. Those late nights in Brussels from 10 years ago when time had lost all meaning. So it seemed it might be on Friday. A press conference scheduled for 12.30pm pushed back a quarter of an hour. And then another 15 minutes. Yet another 15 minutes. There are few things the EU does better than taking negotiations down to the wire. But there the similarities ended. Because when the presser eventually started about an hour later than planned, everything was sweetness and light. António Costa, president of the European Council, Ursula von der Leyen, president of the European Commission, and Andy Burnham presented themselves as the perfect throuple. It had been love at first sight, and they couldn’t wait for their next tryst. They could barely take their eyes off one another. A far cry from the bad old days of Brexit where Theresa May was left on her own with only four pot plants for company. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘They’re struggling for oxygen’: children pay the price as countries allow measles to surge again
articles.description: The US, Mexico and Bolivia this week joined the unenviable club of nations that have lost their measles-free status Deaths caused by measles are not peaceful. In his hospital in Uganda, Dr Eric Wobudeya treats young infants after the virus has attacked their lungs and airways, or triggered pneumonia. “These are children who are dying, and they are struggling for oxygen,” he said. Continue reading...

articles.title: Burnham seals trade and youth mobility deals in biggest step towards EU since Brexit
articles.description: Agreements reached on food and drink, emissions and to allow young people to move around continent, but may be derailed over student fees Andy Burnham has taken the biggest step towards deeper ties with the EU since Brexit, sealing deals to ease trade and create a mobility scheme for young people as he declared a “new world” of cooperation between the two sides. At a major summit in Brussels on Friday the EU and UK announced three deals, on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme, which will allow 100,000 young Britons to live, work, study and travel in the EU, with reciprocal access for Europeans in the UK. Continue reading...

articles.title: Russian missiles and drone hit Poland during attacks on Ukraine
articles.description: Polish PM calls strikes, which took place amid western military exercises, ‘an intentional provocation’ by Moscow Two Russian cruise missiles and a jet-powered drone crashed in Poland, according to officials, during Russian air attacks on Ukraine that took place amid major western military exercises by allied countries. Poland accused Moscow of “provocation” after the strikes in the south-east area of the Nato country. Continue reading...

articles.title: Far-right activist Daniel Thomas jailed for slashing dinghy in Channel

Judge Newton-Price KC described Thomas as a “publicity seeker” who had interfered with the work of law enforcement officers and lifesavers. Continue reading...

articles.title: No one else in Reform is suitable to lead the party, Nigel Farage says
articles.description: Farage issues warning to potential rivals and says he will fight next election as leader if ‘still here and fit and healthy’ Nigel Farage has said he does not see another person who could do his job as leader of Reform UK, in a warning shot to potential rivals who might seek to replace him. The Reform UK leader delivered a message that he was going nowhere despite his worries over his personal safety in the wake of the killing of the Reform politician Ann Widdecombe. Continue reading...

articles.title: Police arrest teacher who missed sentencing after indecent assault conviction
articles.description: Sally-Anne Bowen was found guilty of having sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the 1980s A chemistry teacher who had sexual relationships with two pupils at a boys’ school in the late 1980s has been arrested by police in Hampshire after she failed to turn up to her sentencing hearing. Sally-Anne Bowen, 65, could not be found at her home by Metropolitan police officers on Friday morning after a warrant was issued for her arrest, a court heard. Continue reading...

articles.title: White supremacist convicted of planning bomb attack on asylum seekers in Hull
articles.description: Mikka Anderson stockpiled weapons and tried to recruit accomplice for attack on Royal Hotel A white supremacist has been found guilty of planning a firebomb terror attack on asylum seekers in Hull. Mikka Anderson, 24, stockpiled weapons including napalm, knives and a crossbow for an assault designed to kill as many people as possible, Newcastle crown court heard. Continue reading...

articles.title: Gérard Depardieu and Michel Houellebecq investigated over on-set rape and assault allegations
articles.description: Actor and author are alleged to have attacked and gang-raped a woman while filming together in 2018 French police are investigating allegations that the actor Gérard Depardieu and the author Michel Houellebecq gang-raped and assaulted a woman during a 2018 film shoot. The alleged attack took place in December 2018 during the shooting of Thalasso, a film starring the two men as versions of themselves who meet at a health spa and have long philosophical conversations while in white bath-robes. Continue reading...

articles.title: Friday night will be ‘coldest of the autumn so far’, UK forecasters say
articles.description: Lows will be ‘severe’ in the north, down to -9C, with some sub-zero temperatures farther south Friday night will be the coldest night of the autumn so far, forecasters have said, surpassing the previous chilliest: Thursday. A low of -8.4C was recorded at Tulloch Bridge in the Scottish Highlands overnight, according to the Met Office. Sub-zero temperatures were also recorded in Northern Ireland. More southerly areas stayed substantially warmer overnight on Thursday. Continue reading...

articles.title: Misty-eyed Burnham gambles on closer ties with EU as he throws down gauntlet to Tories and Reform
articles.description: PM challenges rivals to rebuff plan he says could add 0.5% annual growth to economy and offer young people hope Several sentences into a slightly convoluted answer about where UK-EU relations might go next, Andy Burnham abruptly changed tack. “The important point is that the Britain of today and the EU of today is not the one of 2016,” he said. “Life has moved on in so many ways.” This is undoubtedly true. But Burnham’s political gamble on closer ties with Brussels hinges on the assumption that most British voters feel this way as well. Continue reading...

articles.title: Joanne Young’s faith in justice system is sign of real change, but courts are still catching up
articles.description: Young’s abusers were convicted through suspect-centric prosecution, though much more needs to be done for victims Hope can be found in the darkest of places. Joanne Young stood outside Winchester crown court on Thursday and said she was relieved – not just for herself and her family – but for women in the future. Young, who was subjected to years of drugging and rape by her husband , who invited other men to assault her, waived her anonymity to speak out. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cop31 talks go into overtime as debate rages over lack of fossil fuels in draft deal
articles.description: African ministers say they ‘didn’t come here to beg’, with civil society groups calling it the ‘worst Cop ever’ Crucial climate talks headed into overtime on the last official day of the Cop31 UN summit as countries continued to argue over a draft deal that was silent on fossil fuels, with a host of other contentious issues complicating negotiations. Nearly 200 countries struggled to bridge their differences after two weeks of intense talks and impassioned speeches in Antalya, Turkey, about the effects of climate breakdown around the world, with a scheduled finish of Friday evening breached. Continue reading...

articles.title: Cop31 draft climate text dissected: what it says and what it means
articles.description: Fiona Harvey reads between the lines of the draft document that will end up outlining decisions and resolutions from the 31st climate summit Cop31 live – latest updates The final text is one of the most important documents that will come out of the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey. What emerges in the latest draft here is that it will not be a new treaty, but a series of decisions and resolutions. These decisions have legal force in the context of the Paris agreement, so this is a powerful document. But it is also a document that can be accepted only with the consensus of all parties, therefore much of the language is cautious and some is ambiguous or open to interpretation, to the frustration of countries who want to move faster. I. Global progress and context 1. Strongly reaffirms commitment to multilateralism and resolves to remain united in the pursuit of efforts to implement the Convention and achieve the purpose and long-term goals of the Paris Agreement; 2. Recalls that the Paris Agreement will be implemented to reflect equity and the principle of common but differentiated responsibilities and respective capabilities, in the light of different national circumstances; 3. Acknow

articles.title: ‘I went to bed … then Dad called to say Mum was convulsing’ - This is climate breakdown
articles.description: She had been worrying about her elderly parents, but the ferocity of the heatwave took them all by surprise. This is Anne-Sophie Woronoff’s story Location: Besançon, France Disaster: European heatwaves, 2026 Colette Woronoff was one of at least 50,000 people killed by this year’s ferociously hot summer, a modelling study of 854 European cities found last month. The scientists said two in every three of the heat-related deaths resulted from additional warming due to fossil fuel pollution and the destruction of nature. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘The greatest game ever made’: readers and Guardian staff on Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.description: Rockstar’s newest installment of its hit franchise still has plenty of action, along with a dose of ‘healthy masculinity’ Described as the biggest entertainment launch in history, the new Grand Theft Auto game has prompted avid fans around the world to take the day off work, stock up on snacks and celebrate its arrival after 13 years of waiting. While some have already spent hours immersed in the game’s criminal escapades, others have found themselves doing household chores, building houses or simply taking in the scenery – which includes more than 170 flora and fauna species native to Florida . GTA VI has generated extraordinary global anticipation for its action-packed gameplay, but players are now finding new delight in the game’s more intimate moments. Continue reading...

articles.title: Banish the big light: 12 interiors hacks for a cosy winter (and not a candle in sight)
articles.description: From your bath to your bedroom, an experts’ guide to making your home a stylish sanctuary We are in the midst of “staying-in season”, enduring cold days and long nights. But if your attempts at hibernation aren’t working, maybe the ambience is off. The gloomy winter months call for soft mood lighting, warmer textures and sunny colours to bring more joy into your home. From accessories that tell a story to the trending fabric trick to hide clutter, here are ways to create that elusive sense of cosiness this season. And I promise none of them involves buying yet another candle. *** Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘It’s peak Aussie – and it’s fantastic!’ How Australian TV conquered the world
articles.description: From Colin from Accounts to a certain blue heeler dog, Australian TV has swept the globe – so much so that many kids have picked up the accent. Homegrown stars and creators explain how down under went overground About four years ago, parents around the world began observing a strange phenomena in their children: Australian accents. Bluey – the charming cartoon about a dog and her family that is currently one of the most watched shows in the world – had children saying words such as “dunny” and “brekky” without thinking twice. “When I was a kid, I would do an American accent when I played with my toys,” says Daley Pearson, co-founder of Ludo Studio, which makes Bluey. “So this is like the colony taking back over!” Continue reading...

articles.title: Melania: the series review – so bad it robbed me of my capacity to discern time and space
articles.description: The first lady’s two-part TV documentary is a dead-eyed advert that barely manages to masquerade as entertainment. Calling it thin gruel would be an insult to the gruel industry Previously on Melania: earlier this year – either because it found her a compelling subject, or because it wanted to flatter the president before a potentially destructive upcoming antitrust trial – Amazon spent $75m (£57m) to make and market a theatrically released documentary about Melania Trump. I’m telling you this for two reasons. First, because you didn’t watch the Melania film. Nobody did, except for journalists who sat in otherwise empty cinemas and (if reports are to believed) people who responded to Craigslist ads offering them $50 to see it. The second reason is because Melania is a series now. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘You can’t get experience if no one’s employing you’: the vicious circle facing Blackpool’s Neets
articles.description: The English seaside town tops the list for 16- to 24-year-olds out of work and education, but not for lack of young jobseekers’ efforts Speaking random words like “cat” and “box” into her phone while filming herself in her pyjamas, Amy Butterworth’s relentless search for a job had reached a new level of absurdity. The 19-year-old from Blackpool was applying for a role at Marks & Spencer, but first had to prove she was not a robot. Continue reading...

articles.title: The week around the world in 20 pictures
articles.description: Trump in China, blackouts in Kyiv, Israeli strikes in Gaza and the launch of Grand Theft Auto VI – the past seven days as captured by the world’s leading photojournalists Warning: this gallery contains images some readers may find distressing Continue reading...

articles.title: Vitamin D, fiber and flavor: how healthy are mushrooms?
articles.description: Experts say there are many reasons to boost our consumption of mushrooms and incorporate them into our diets Mushrooms aren’t quite as popular in the US as they are in other parts of the world . On average, Americans eat just shy of 4lb (1.81kg) of mushrooms per capita each year, while in South Korea people eat almost 6lb (2.72kg) a year, and in Japan, that number is closer to 12lb (5.44kg). People in the US also don’t consume as wide a variety of mushrooms as other parts of the world, says Dr Krystle Zuniga, a board-certified oncology dietitian based in Austin, Texas. “I often think of them as a forgotten vegetable,” she says, though she clarifies they are technically fungi. Continue reading...

articles.title: Suki Waterhouse and Robert Pattinson to become Britain’s next big Hollywood power couple
articles.description: Duo’s fame set to soar after Pattinson announced as next James Bond – but they will take newgen approach to power He is the next James Bond. She is a successful model/actor/singer-songwriter. Together, they are set to become the next big British power couple in Hollywood. articles.title: Forget rogue robots, it’s tech billionaires and AI cricket that should really terrify us | Barney Ronay
articles.description: The encroachment of artificial intelligence smells like the death of sport. Can we find the will and collective backbone to resist? There was an interesting development this week in the endless rolling mega-froth over tech billionaire Jensen Huang , a saga that may or may not have involved some kind of adulterous 63-year-old honey trap spy dynamic . The latest suggestion being punted about is that, whatever his raw human frailties, Huang is in fact “irreplaceable” as the president of Nvidia. Only this guy can do it. Only this leather-jacketed human visionary, who looks in every available photo like your GCSE chemistry teacher’s profile pic on TerrifiedUkrainianSinglesWantToDateYou.com, can manage this key artificial intelligence mission. Continue reading...

articles.title: After Russell Brand, and now another horrific rape verdict, shame really does have to change sides | Jonathan Freedland
articles.description: From predatory male celebrities to ordinary men who connive to abuse women, there is no doubt where the problem lies – and the solution too The only thing they have in common is that they are men. Those convicted of the rape and sexual assault of Joanne Young – who was drugged by her husband, so that he could offer her unconscious body to strangers – do not come from one class or ethnic group or age cohort. Like the 50 men convicted alongside Dominique Pelicot for the serial rape of his wife, Gisèle, which this case resembles, they run the full range. Young’s oldest abuser is now 62, her youngest was 22. The four convicted on Thursday included two who were white, two who were not. Among them was a former music producer, a taxi driver and a one-time contractor for the Ministry of Defence. The only thing they have in common is that they are men. That closes off a delusion that many reach for when confronted with heinous crimes committed against women: the claim that such appalling acts are peculiar to a specific category of man. Last week, the focus was on famous men, prompted by the rape conviction of Russell Brand and the allegations of underage grooming and predatory behaviour by

articles.title: Digested week: Pity the touring royals – and the hacks made to schlep around after them
articles.description: It’s a hard life for the Prince and Princess of Wales, but spare a thought too for jailed Bankman-Fried and the overlooked 007s All eyes on China ahead of the trilateral summit this week, but it’s India and the three-day royal tour by the Prince and Princess of Wales that catches my eye. The couple arrive in Mumbai and as a steady stream of photos emanates from their back-to-back schedule, the usual question surfaces: how on earth do they stand it? Continue reading...

articles.title: Delays mean Robert Pattinson doesn’t have to do a third Batman movie. DC Studios had better persuade him – and fast
articles.description: The actor’s new role as James Bond could be bad news for DC, as a new owner, new chief and new director already threaten to shake and stir Gotham’s distinctive hero Can one actor play both Batman and James Bond? This is the question many have been asking since Robert Pattinson was announced as the new 007 . The obvious answer is yes: the 40-year-old Englishman has the poise, charisma and steel to join His Majesty’s Secret Service, and saving Gotham could soon become something he fits in between assignments. Among all the furore over Pattinson’s appointment, it would have been easy to miss some rather less cheering news for the citizens of Gotham. According to the Wrap , delays to The Batman: Part II have freed the actor from his contractual obligation to make a third film. The sequel is now due in February 2028, almost six years after the first instalment. He could still sign a new deal, of course, but Warner Bros will have to persuade its caped crusader to stick around. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
articles.description: It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory. Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage admits that Brexit was botched. But he wants greater divergence from, rather than incr

articles.title: The Guardian view on Jan van Eyck’s portraits: what it means to be human | Editorial
articles.description: A tiny scar, bloodshot eyes and sagging jowls – it is the intimate details of these 15th-century masterpieces that make them so relatable today The word “human” may have been crowned the Cambridge dictionary’s word of 2026 , but its meaning is nowhere more manifest than in an exhibition of paintings from almost 600 years ago. Humanness is captured in every pore and wrinkle of all nine of Jan van Eyck ’s portraits, united for the first time by the National Gallery. The paintings have been loaned from Berlin, Vienna, Dresden, Bruges and Sibiu in Romania, in a triumph of cultural exchange that proves the blockbuster show is still very much alive. And so, it almost seems, are the people depicted in it, who appear so real we might “recognise them on the tube”, as the exhibition’s co-curator Nicholas Flory put it , even given their extravagant headgear. A purplish wart, a tiny scar, bloodshot eyes, sagging jowls and dirty fingernails – it is the intimate details of Van Eyck’s likenesses that transformed Renaissance portraiture and make his sitters so relatable, in modern parlance, today. Like a novelist, the artist wanted to create the impression of capturing his subjects in a moment in

articles.title: We should be free to call ourselves Black English | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to an article about categories on the census form It’s about time we fixed the Black English category in the census, whether popular or not ( It’s absurd that ‘Black English’ is not on the census. We should be free to claim that identity if we choose, 14 November ). Categories count. They make citizens, politically engineer belonging and allow people to be seen and to see themselves. The excuse that the Black English category is simply unpopular doesn’t wash. I remember in the 1990s when the Black British, or Black African categories were all the rage, they were never particularly comfortable to tick, but we all got over ourselves and stomached the flattening of our complex identities for what we believed was a good cause. A Black English category would also help me out enormously, living as I do in France, where people don’t believe me when I say I’m English, but simply think I’m deluded and can’t speak French properly – which I can. Having left Scotland when I was three and grown up in London, I felt I couldn’t legitimately call myself Scottish – but English, I could. Years ago I stopped calling myself Britannique , because Black or otherwise, it just didn’t reall

articles.title: Judges, juries and rape myths in trials | Letters
articles.description: Paul Keleher KC offers an insight into how juries are directed. Plus a letter from Prof Nicole Moreham In your report ( ‘Pull back the curtain’ on treatment of sexual assault victims in court, says UK government adviser, 15 November ), Prof Katrin Hohl suggests that while significant progress has been made by police forces and the Crown Prosecution Service, the court system was being left behind. It seems to be little known that for many years judges have been trained to direct juries to ignore rape myths and direct them that many victims of sexual assault are unable to physically resist and often delay reporting the assault. Juries are directed that this should not cast doubt on their accounts of being assaulted. Continue reading...

articles.title: It’s time we all made healthy food go further | Letters
articles.description: Estelle Herszenhorn says the food we throw away at home costs an average household of four around £1,000 a year, while Lily van den Broecke and Charlie Wartnaby share tea ideas Rachel Dixon’s article ( The root-to-tip revolution! An A-Z of how to eat plants in full – for extra flavour, fibre and savings, 17 November ) shows how we can make healthy food go further, and the opportunity is bigger than many of us realise. The food we throw away at home costs an average household of four around  £1,000 a year , and much of it is good fruit and vegetables that could have been eaten. It’s not just peel and stalks we bin. WRAP found that date labels on fresh produce got in the way of people’s judgment, so more people said they would throw it out. Retailers have since removed those labels at scale, making it easier for all of us to use more of what we buy by default, and WRAP estimates that could save 50,000 tonnes a year. Continue reading...

articles.title: The best way to avoid winter illness | Letters
articles.description: Responding to an article in the series The experts, Sally Billenness advocates wearing a mask and ensuring good ventilation. Plus, a letter by Caroline Clitter “Stay hydrated”, “keep moisturised”, “go for a walk”, “be social”: while these are definitely good things for us to do, they are hardly the top of the list for avoiding winter ailments ( Get vaccinated, don’t vape – and moisturise liberally! 10 doctors on how to avoid and treat winter ailments, 18 November ). I am glad you have included vaccinations, but the two most useful things you can do don’t get a mention: wear a mask and ensure ventilation. It’s flu season and airborne viruses such as Covid are still harming people, although as it is hardly ever reported you would not know it. People are being told that “it’s fine”, but as a long-Covid sufferer for 2.5 years, I can tell you this disease is vile: I wouldn’t wish it on my worst enemy, certainly not my loved ones. I am unable to go for a walk, be social or stay active. If people feel ill (even “just a cold”) they should stay at home and avoid spreading their germs to everyone they meet, because they probably won’t know who is vulnerable. Sally Billenness Hounslow, London

articles.title: Training hard and biding his time, Dele Alli has not given up on football yet
articles.description: The 30-year-old former England star combines Twitch streaming with working to return to the top as a player Consider the training regime Dele Alli has followed since he left Como 18 months ago and it becomes clear why he takes exception to suggestions he has given up on football in favour of becoming an internet personality. He trains five or six days a week with Connor Peters, an elite performance coach who has worked with players including Trevoh Chalobah. They spend four days on the pitch and days in between in the gym. A typical day begins at 9am with an hour of activation and stretching before Dele heads to non-league Windsor & Eton at 11am, where he trains on the pitches and uses the facilities. Then it’s back home to use his own oxygen chamber and sauna for a recovery session. Continue reading...

articles.title: Pochettino the connector: will human touch lift Manchester United?
articles.description: Argentinian has excelled in man-management – but will need his powers to energise new squad and impress owners Mauricio Pochettino celebrated his 50th birthday in style. It was March 2022, he was in charge at Paris Saint-Germain and the venue was a stunning boutique hotel; the kind that many capitals have but only Paris truly does . Pochettino’s family and friends were there. So were his inner coaching circle, who are basically family. There were lots of people from PSG. And a good time was had by all. For Pochettino, it was emotional. As everybody knows, the new Manchester United head coach is the kind of guy to well up when the speeches start, so imagine how he felt when he looked up at the big screen and a video montage of well-wishers started to roll. Continue reading...

articles.title: The Super Bowl of F1: how Las Vegas GP has hit the jackpot after turbulent start
articles.description: George Russell calls it the biggest race on the Formula One calendar bar Monaco – and the numbers back him up That Formula One has achieved a palpable success in hosting a race in Las Vegas is impossible to ignore. Even with this year’s outing a dead rubber and with the city in perhaps its least flattering light, the cold drizzle of a Thursday afternoon beneath gunmetal-grey skies, the fans who have flocked to Nevada were irrepressibly enthusiastic. Long queues stretched out into the streets before the gates were even open and it seems many locals who were initially cool to the somewhat disruptive F1 circus have embraced the fans, their fervour for the sport and the positive impact of the race. articles.title: Death threats to Bowens revealed after De Boinville security incident
articles.description: Abuse and threats are becoming a grimly familiar part of daily routine for riders, confirms jockeys’ association When Nico de Boinville received a security escort back to his car after racing at Plumpton on Monday, following a telephone threat to harm the jockey received at Nicky Henderson’s stable, it was the first time that such a move had received widespread media attention. It was not, however, the first time that it had been felt necessary to give a rider additional protection at a racecourse. James Bowen said on Friday, in a blog for the bookmaker Dragonsports, that he and his brother, Sean, the champion over jumps, “were both the subject of death threats” during a meeting at Ffos Las in October 2025, “to the extent that we had security accompanying us between the paddock and weighing room for the next three or four days.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Victor Wembanyama has turned his NBA finals humiliation into a revenge tour for the ages
articles.description: After a humiliating NBA finals defeat, the 22-year-old has returned with a vengeance – and the Spurs look like contenders again It wouldn’t be exactly right to say Victor Wembanyama didn’t miss a beat after a disastrous NBA finals in June that left him and his San Antonio Spurs defeated, memed and embarrassed. In the Spurs’ first game this season, against an Oklahoma City Thunder team since decimated by injuries, Wemby went an appalling 1-for-13 from the field. Ten of his 12 points came via free throws. After getting blocked by Aday Mara, he leaned over his knees and muttered furiously to himself as if trying to exorcise an intrusive thought. It brought to mind an image from the NBA finals a few months earlier: Wemby on the floor after being fouled by the Knicks’ Mitchell Robinson, crowing, “I’m in your head!” The Spurs went on to blow a 29-point lead , lose the game and the finals. Now Wemby seemed too preoccupied with the issues within his own dome to worry about wreaking havoc in anybody else’s. Game two saw Wembanyama elect to lay the ball up instead of dunking it in the dying seconds of a close tilt with the Houston Rockets, which the springy Amen Thompson blocked spectacularl

articles.title: UK operation wards off risk of cyber-attack on supermarket fridges and freezers
articles.description: News of vulnerability comes after retailers in at least seven European countries hit by cyber-attacks A secret government cybersecurity operation recently warded off the risk of a cyber-attack on fridges and freezers in UK supermarkets, warehouses, restaurants, petrol stations and stadiums, it has emerged. An attack would have been similar to those that have caused many millions of euros of damage in continental Europe in recent months. But, while many retailers have now been protected, researchers warned that many more could still be vulnerable. Continue reading...

articles.title: Two men killed after glider crashes into Loch Leven in Scotland
articles.description: The pair had taken off from the Scottish Gliding Centre at nearby Portmoak on a training flight Two men have been killed after their glider crashed into Loch Leven, a large body of water in Perth and Kinross, on Friday morning. articles.title: Young people across Europe stage coordinated ‘fight for our future’ protests

Continue reading...

articles.title: JP Morgan boss says he will find ways to offset ‘unfair’ rise in UK tax on banks
articles.description: Jamie Dimon says he is ‘setting an example’ in seeking to claw back Labour’s increase in surcharge, from 3% to 6% Jamie Dimon, the chief executive of JP Morgan, has said he will find ways to offset the chancellor’s tax rise for banks, calling the increase unfair. articles.title: Spain frees wealthy US-sought activist on bail as Irish police raid Dublin home
articles.description: Pro-Palestinian donor James ‘Fergie’ Chambers released as court considers extradition request In a blur of events surrounding the Trump administration’s effort to extradite James “Fergie” Chambers, Spain released the wealthy US activist and donor on bail even as Irish police raided a Dublin house owned by Chambers and his partner, Stella Schnabel, acting on a request from US authorities. Continue reading...

articles.title: Home Alone sequel reportedly in development with Macaulay Culkin returning

articles.title: Zohran Mamdani unveils plan to close Rikers Island jail complex
articles.description: Mayor plans to close jail by 2032 and relocate its remaining population to smaller facilities across four boroughs Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island jail complex, with a goal to end all incarceration at the current facility and relocate its remaining jail population by the end of 2032. “It is time to finally close Rikers Island,” Mamdani said in a statement. “For decades, New Yorkers have demanded a correctional system that is safe and humane. This plan puts us on a path to deliver just that: closing Rikers, reducing pretrial detention, tackling the case delays that deprive people of their right to a speedy trial and investing $146m in the evidence-based supports that helps break the cycles of incarceration.” Continue reading...

articles.title: Is Claude creator Anthropic really worth $1.3 trillion? - The Latest
articles.description: The AI firm and Claude chatbot maker Anthropic has made a historic stock market debut, with a peak valuation of $1.3tn on its first day of trading.
