Despite the excitement, the Guardian’s head of business John Collingridge tells Lucy Hough that there are still challenges ahead for the global AI industry Continue reading...

articles.title: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China

articles.description: Young Vic, London Adaptation of Christian Kracht’s novel is full of heartwarming comedy as a mother and son take a trip to distribute ‘dirty money’ to good causes You would be hard-pushed to find a more charismatic double act than Kathryn Hunter and Ben Whishaw. She dazzles as a dowager, bringing flamboyant physical flourishes as she knocks back the cooking wine; he is her lugubrious son, Christian, a novelist with writer’s block. Their story trades on kookiness but the chemistry would keep you captivated even if they watched paint dry for the duration of this interval-free drama. Based on Swiss author Christian Kracht’s bestselling novel, adapted by Colin Teevan, it is charmingly directed by Walter Meierjohann. The third big star is Lizzie Clachan’s set, so full of mischief that it is like a magician pulling out imaginative visual jokes and clever thrills and spills. Glyn Pritchard heroically plays ancillary roles (from taxi driver to waiter) with lightning-quick wardrobe changes while the sound effects are visibly, wittily created in a glass studio. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘If they play dirty, we’ll be total and utter filth!’ Gasp-inducing sex-and-scandal drama War is here to stay
articles.description: Dominic West and Sienna Miller’s divorce battle has made for a rollicking potboiler in prestige drama clothing. As it approaches its explosive finale, expect the show to become a TV fixture A tech titan is brought down by the oldest trick in the book: a honeytrap. In the week that Nvidia’s Jensen Huang , co-founder of the world’s most valuable chip company, worth a whopping $4tn (£3tn), resigned over revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, divorce drama War could hardly feel more timely. That’s also how the HBO/Sky legal thriller begins. Billionaire social media mogul Morgan Henderson (Dominic West in textbook posh rotter mode) has a hotel tryst with an alluring stranger after an awards show. She turns out to be in cahoots with his wife, Hollywood star Carla Duval (played with icy glamour by Sienna Miller), to prove her husband’s infidelity. Mission most definitely accomplished. Continue reading...

articles.title: The week’s best new tracks and the act you need to know: the rangy folk-prog songwriting of Threshold
articles.description: Isaac Eiger’s solo venture leaves jangle pop behind for a wilder sound. Often it owes a debt to Alex G, but what indie-rock song doesn’t these days? From New York via Montana Recommended if you like Cameron Winter, Tobias Jesso Jr, Alex G Up next Supporting Caroline on tour in Canada and the US until 19 November Isaac Eiger is something of a scene legend in the world of American indie-rock. Raised in Bozeman, Montana, he was the founder and lead singer of the cult shoegaze-adjacent six-piece Strange Ranger, who left heartbroken a small, fervent fanbase when they announced their breakup in 2023. Taking a discernibly British approach to their sound, Strange Ranger traversed C86-y jangle-pop before landing on Madchester rave-up for their final album, 2023’s Pure Music. But Eiger is nothing if not musically worldly: he has written and produced with both underground heroes (Cassandra Jenkins, Chanel Beads) and nascent pop stars (Adéla, Frost Children). Ever-prolific, Eiger also has a solo project under the name Threshold, with which he released a gauzy, 19-minute EP in 2024 called Thief. articles.title: The best recent crime and thrillers – review roundup
articles.description: The Taper Man by Nick Harkaway; Watch the Quiet Snow by Mick Herron; Revenge Plot by Stephanie Wrobel; The Voices of the Dead by Nicola Upson; The Bells of Fortune by Leonora Nattrass The Taper Man by Nick Harkaway (Viking, £22) The second George Smiley continuation novel from John le Carré’s son Nick Harkaway is set in 1965 and features early iterations of several characters who appear in Tinker Tailor Soldier Spy and Smiley’s People. The cold war is at its height, and British intelligence is keen to protect one of its most important sources, Red Army general Vladimir Vasilev. When a colleague is shot in Helsinki, Smiley discovers a connection to a group of Soviet agents who, through their links to a now defunct spying operation in the US, may jeopardise this key asset. Smiley travels to California to find the “Taper Man”, a sleeper agent whose job is to remain behind when the rest of the network is burned. Meanwhile, leftwing academic Roy Bland goes undercover in Moscow, but things do not go according to plan. Intricately plotted and densely written, The Taper Man takes time to get going, with a fair bit of cold war history and analysis to be digested, but it is a worthy and welc

articles.title: Roll up, roll up! Marc Chagall’s Circus is the most mesmerising big top you’ve ever seen – review
articles.description: Hepworth Wakefield, West Yorkshire He spent over 60 years painting clowns, ringmasters and acrobats – and the results transport you to a dazzling magical world At the opening of The Circus, a self-portrait of Marc Chagall is placed next to a lithograph of a clown. The portrait is small and sketched simply in a blue crayon, as if Chagall had quickly dashed it out to pacify an inquisitive fan. In contrast, the clown is rich in colour and texture, with a heavily detailed backdrop of musicians, spectators and performers. But there is something uncanny about this pairing, created more than 40 years apart. They both wear small, brimmed hats with hair springing out from underneath, and their facial expressions are somewhat inscrutable. It is the perfect introduction to an exhibition that explores Chagall’s lifelong fascination with the circus, both as a subject and as a symbolic motif. In placing Chagall and the clown side by side, we understand this immediately – the clown is both a clown and a metaphor for the artist. In his 1967 art book Cirque, Chagall writes: “This clown – he is he and I.” Continue reading...

articles.title: You shall go to the panto! Northern Ballet’s Cinderella spices the fairytale with festive fun – and a sweet twist
articles.description: Norwich Theatre Royal Magic is sprinkled over Michael Pink’s elegant show, with the spirited score played by the Northern Ballet Sinfonia It wouldn’t be the first time an ugly sister has stolen the show. Andrew Tomlinson is a hoot in Northern Ballet’s new Cinderella as a klutzy, vainglorious stepsister with a great line in lovably grotesque facial expressions. He certainly provides some panto-like festivity in the midst of an otherwise very nice ballet. Getting its UK premiere, this pretty Cinderella is choreographed by Michael Pink, who was associate artistic director at Northern Ballet in the 1990s, and it feels very much like the Northern Ballet of old: accessible and enjoyable mainstream dance with clear storytelling. (It was originally made for Milwaukee Ballet, where Pink has been artistic director since 2002.) Continue reading...

articles.title: Now get out of that! How can the new James Bond film get around 007’s death in No Time to Die?
articles.description: Was it all a dream? Has Bond been in hiding? Or will Robert Pattinson simply report to HR on his first day? Russell T Davies, David Hare and more give their takes “James Bond will return,” says the closing title on No Time to Die, the most recent James Bond film and the final one to star Daniel Craig. It is just as well: Bond has to all appearances been vaporised by sea-launched missiles, having been infected by nanobots programmed to attack his nearest and dearest at the slightest touch. No one would believe that one of the world’s most successful film series would come to such an abrupt halt, but no doubt a little reassurance helped. Nevertheless, the first order of business for scriptwriter Steven Knight and director Denis Villeneuve will be dealing with it: how to revive and re-energise a character at the heart of the action. Speculation on their best way forward has been rife, and previous examples are not hard to find. Sherlock Holmes was killed off by Arthur Conan Doyle by fighting his arch enemy Professor Moriarty at the Reichenbach Falls in the story The Final Problem, only to resuscitate him a decade later with The Adventure of the Empty House. articles.title: The best Black Friday beauty deals I’d actually buy, from LED face masks to skincare staples
articles.description: We’ve rounded up the beauty and hair care offers that are actually worth it – all tried, tested and loved by us • The best early Black Friday deals Few of us may be able to justify the cost of a big-ticket TV this Black Friday, but beauty is one area where we can usually afford a treat or two. Thank you, lipstick effect . It can feel like a no-brainer to stock up on our regular favourites and get a few Christmas presents crossed off the list while prices are lower. But deals do something funky to our brains. Retailers know how to lure us in, using big discounts and “selling fast” pop-ups that cause our typically rational brains to short circuit. Add a high-pressure countdown, and before you know it, you’ve been enticed into buying countless products you didn’t set out to buy. Impulse beauty buys are easy to regret later when you snap back into consciousness – not only because of the money you’ve spent, but also because of the waste they create. Continue reading...

articles.title: Bill’s Included review – Rob Brydon’s new character is as glorious as Gavin & Stacey’s Uncle Bryn
articles.description: The comic is sublime as a middle-aged landlord attempting to befriend student tenants. It’s very sweet – but the storylines and supporting characters are flimsy to say the least Bill Beam (Rob Brydon) is a chump, a sap, a bejumpered limpet clinging to the peripheries of his own existence. “I’m being left behind,” he tells best friend Drew (Kevin Eldon) who, having heard this – and that, and the other – a thousand times before, stifles a well-earned yawn. Bill’s wife has left him for the gardener (“No hard feelings!”) and lo, this ever-dimming bulb of cable-knit neediness must find a solution to both his newfound “cashflow crisis” and deepening existential haplessness. What to do? Enter, stage left, a fire at the local student halls and, with it, an answer to the plonker’s prayers: Bill will rent out his spare bedrooms to four undergraduates. Yes! This will provide him with the requisite dosh, a much-needed sense of purpose and a fresh audience for his piping-hot takes on Jeremy Beadle, the big Asda and the fact that his phone number is “one of only nine UK landlines to conclude with the digits 1, 2, 3, 4.” Go tell it on the mountain! But bring a sad trombone while you’re at it. Bec

articles.title: Dmitri Kasterine obituary
articles.description: Photographer who captured the humanity of subjects including Queen Elizabeth II, Dirk Bogarde, Jean-Michel Basquiat and Tom Stoppard In 1963, the photographer Dmitri Kasterine heard that Stanley Kubrick was in London filming Dr Strangelove. Kasterine was a fan, so he approached the editor of Queen magazine and successfully pitched a feature on the director at work. Kubrick noticed him on set and said: “Would you like to come and work for me? You stand in the right place.” Kasterine worked for Kubrick from 1963 to 1971, taking the stills on Dr Strangelove, 2001: A Space Odyssey and A Clockwork Orange. Kubrick taught the photographer the importance of courage, patience and perseverance. Continue reading...

To facilitate the laying of this new watermain, a lane closure will be in place around each working area and signage will be in place. The work, which involves laying around 170 metres of new watermain between Carnhill Roundabout and Greenhaw Road, will replace a section of the 50-year-old Ballyarnett Water Trunkmain which has been prone to bursts. The upgrade will help to protect homes from flooding, should a burst occur in the future, and provide improved access for NI Water maintenance. A l ane closure controlled by temporary traffic lights will be in place on Racecourse Road around the working area from Monday 27 th July for four weeks. A further two weeks of work will take place in the adjacent verge which will not require any traffic management. Temporary traffic lights will be manned during peak hours and access to properties will be maintained at all times, although parking spaces within the working area will be temporarily unavailable. Once the lane closure is removed, works will move into the adjacent verge to complete the final phase of w

articles.title: Craigavon - Closure of Maple Path & Parkmore Footbridges
articles.description: Closure of Maple Path and Parkmore Footbridges, Craigavon The Department for Infrastructure have announced that the Maple Path and Parkmore footbridges in Craigavon will be closed from Thursday 4 June 2026. Detailed engineering inspections identified structural concerns, and it has been concluded that the closure of these footbridges is necessary while a permanent solution is developed. Alternative local walking routes are available and will be signposted where appropriate. While these routes may increase journey times for some users, they will provide access around the affected areas. The Department recognises the importance of both footbridges to local residents and apologises for any inconvenience caused. However, as the Department’s infrastructure assets age there will always be an eventual need to replace structures that present safety issues or have come to the end of their natural lifespan. Further information on future proposals for the bridges will be provided as work progresses. The Department would like to thank the public for their patience and cooperation.

articles.title: Pump Prices Hit Eight-Month Low Ahead Of Thanksgiving Travel
articles.description: Pump Prices Hit Eight-Month Low Ahead Of Thanksgiving Travel With Thanksgiving next week, the holiday travel period is about to begin.  There is some good news Thursday morning: the latest AAA data shows the national average price of gasoline at US pumps has slipped to its lowest level since mid-March, or about three weeks into "Operation Epic Fury"... Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union, pointed out on X this morning that while everyone is glued to their Bloomberg Terminals awaiting the first trade in the blockbuster Anthropic IPO , pump prices also deserve attention. "I know everyone is watching Anthropic today, but take a look at gas prices. Gas price (national average) today: $3.72. This is the lowest price since March 16 ," Long said. articles.title: I’m really hurt that my parents didn’t give me a 40th birthday gift | Ask Annalisa Barbieri
articles.description: You feel overlooked, but your parents’ disappointing behaviour does not necessarily mean they don’t love you I turned 40 a few years ago . For my 21st and 30th birthdays I got jewellery from my parents, so when they didn’t ask what I wanted, I assumed they would follow this tradition. But I got nothing. Not even an apology. It later transpired that they thought I was turning 41. But even then to receive nothing is hurtful . They blamed it on old age and said they had been struggling with their health. I place a lot of importance on gift giving . It isn’t about the value, but it’s nice to feel someone has spent time thinking about you . To get nothing just screamed that they didn’t care. Continue reading...

articles.title: How the war in Iran turned the Gulf into a climate catastrophe – video explainer
articles.description: The war between the US, Israel and Iran has turned the strait of Hormuz, one of the world’s busiest oil shipping routes, into a battlefield, but also the centre of a deepening environmental disaster. Tankers struck by missiles or sea mines are leaking oil into the Gulf, leaving vast slicks visible from space, staining coastlines and threatening lasting damage to marine ecosystems. Many of these areas remain inaccessible because of the naval blockade, making it virtually impossible to document the devastation on the ground. The Guardian has examined dozens of satellite images and spoken to environmental experts in an effort to assess the scale of the damage Oil slicks seen from space: the devastating impact of boat strikes on fragile Gulf ecosystems Continue reading...

articles.description: PG&E Gave $1 Million To Newsom's Orbit, Then Got Its Bailout Authored by Christopher F. Rufo, Susan Crabtree, and Kenneth Schrupp via City Journal , Paradise, California was a quiet town in the Sierra Nevada foothills. Seniors flocked there seeking affordable homes. Others came for abundant land and small-town charm. For more than a century, Paradise was an oasis from the hustle of urban California. On November 8, 2018, it all came crashing down. A hook, suspended from a tower owned by Pacific Gas and Electric, one of America's largest utilities, snapped. A jumper conductor hit the tower, melting metal strands and setting nearby vegetation ablaze. Paradise and its surroundings were destroyed: 150,000 acres were incinerated, thousands of homes were leveled, and 85 people were killed. The town's population shrunk by more than half in the five years that followed the infamous Camp Fire. PG&E eventually pleaded guilty to 84 counts of manslaughter. In the wake of the disaster, PG&E found itself on the hook for more than $10 billion in damages and insurance claims. articles.title: Russia To Let Retail Investors Trade Bitcoin On Margin
articles.description: Russia To Let Retail Investors Trade Bitcoin On Margin Authored by Micah Zimmerman via Bitcoin Magazine , Russia's central bank plans to let ordinary investors trade bitcoin and other crypto on margin, capped at 300,000 rubles with a broker , a senior Bank of Russia official said this week, days after retail buying became legal. Olga Shishlyannikova, director of the central bank's department of investment financial intermediaries, outlined the plan at the Ural Conference hosted by NAUFOR, the national association of securities market participants, RBC Investments reported. She said the margin rule and two other acts are under review at Russia's Justice Ministry, and the regulator expects them to be registered by the end of 2026 . It is not yet clear whether the 300,000-ruble margin limit for non-qualified investors will be shared with the existing cap on crypto purchases or counted separately. The central bank first published draft margin rules in July. Under that draft, brokers could accept cryptocurrencies as collateral for margin positions, and their clients could sell short . articles.title: Taiwan Strangles The Shorts After The Taiex Loses 5,000 Points In Three Days
articles.description: Taiwan Strangles The Shorts After The Taiex Loses 5,000 Points In Three Days Regulators don't cut a short-selling quota twice in two weeks because the first cut worked. On Thursday, hours after the Taiex plunged 1,768 points or 4.4% to 38,426.89, and the small-cap TPEx crashed 7.2% with more than 280 OTC names locked limit-down, Taiwan's Financial Supervisory Commission tightened the screws again: the intraday cap on short sales of borrowed shares drops from 3% to just 1% of a stock's 30-day average daily volume , and any stock that falls 3.5% or more in a session (down from 10%, i.e. limit-down) can't be shorted below the prior close the next day. The new rules take effect Friday, November 20, according to Goldman's securities lending desk and the FSC's own notice, in what Goldman's Peter Slater calls the second "Short Sell Ban" in as many weeks. As of Thursday's close, that trigger alone covers more than a thousand listed and OTC names, local press reported. This is the second clampdown this month. As regular readers will recall, when the AI unwind sent Taipei into a bear market on November 6, the FSC cut the quota from 30% to 3% and lifted the short-sale margin to 130% from 90%

articles.title: My search for Bologna’s perfect tagliatelle al ragù - the real ‘spag bol’
articles.description: The signature dish of Italy’s gastronomic capital is taken far more seriously than its British derivative. So which restaurant does the best ‘tag rag’? I used to eat spag bol three times a week. I’d have it every Friday at my nan’s, every Saturday at my dad’s, and every Tuesday at my mum’s. My nan would lean heavily on Dolmio and add a cheeky splash of Tabasco. My mum would rustle up hers in the time it took the pasta to cook, which gave it a crunchiness that sometimes made me cry (I swear to God, those onions were practically raw). And my dad would let his bubble away for the duration of Gladiators, meaning that by the time it was dished up at the start of Blind Date, it had an intensity that felt positively foreign. I’m not alone in being a big fan of spag bol – the dish is often voted the nation’s favourite, and there’s now even a National Spaghetti Bolognese Day (22 May) – but I do sometimes wonder what it is about this relatively simple import, essentially a combo of mince and tomatoes plonked upon pasta, that has won over millions and withstood the vagaries of time. So I travelled to the dish’s motherland, Bologna, to unlock its secrets and hunt down some prime examples. Cont

articles.title: Don’t buy new tech this Black Friday: expert tips for buying refurbished phones and laptops
articles.description: Tech on its last legs? Refurbished can be the cheaper, greener option. Here’s how to choose well and avoid the pitfalls • How to make your phone last longer • The best sustainable Black Friday deals Even if you do your best to avoid it, it’s hard to escape the noise of retailers offering implausible-seeming Black Friday discounts on desirable technology. What they won’t be so keen to highlight is the huge environmental cost that comes from feeding the capitalist beast year on year, given what an obvious sales vibe-killer it would be. While the best approach for the planet is to opt out completely and observe the alternative holiday of Buy Nothing Day instead, such an approach can prove self-defeating for your finances in the long term. If you shop smart on Black Friday and avoid the lure of impulse buys, it’s a good time to stock up on the things you need at lower prices than the rest of the year. Continue reading...

articles.title: Life insurance: what is it and do you need it?

articles.title: I jumped from a plane at 12,000ft. In mid-air, a friend’s knee collided into my neck
articles.description: A group of eight trainee parachutists did the jump, and not far from the ground, disaster struck. Rob Bugden describes how he rebuilt his life after the accident that changed everything The skydive was going to plan. At 12,000ft, Rob Bugden jumped from the plane, quickly getting himself stable by arching his back to create a solid base. He checked for speed and altitude on his watch, and when he was low enough, pulled the parachute’s toggles. “I looked up. Good canopy.” But then: “Cut to black. And I’m waking up in a hospital in Phoenix.” It was 21 January 2016, the final day of his Royal Air Force high altitude training in the US, when 30-year-old Bugden collided – mid-air – with his friend, Brook Stebbings. They were moving into the landing stack formation, a vertical queue of eight parachutists flying in a holding pattern at different altitudes, when, at approximately 1,000ft, Stebbings’ knee crashed into him, breaking his neck. They fell to the sand in the middle of the desert, entangled – looking, according to the team on the ground, “like we had a bag of washing above our heads”. Continue reading...

articles.title: You Can See Everything review – unblinking, unhinged and unmissable
articles.description: Nathan Fielder’s intense close-range study of fraudster Elizabeth Holmes is as gripping as any thriller • This review contains spoilers Thrillingly reckless, deliciously irresponsible and as gripping as any thriller, this situationist docu-hybrid masterpiece from co-directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim gets up close and personal with convicted fraudster Elizabeth Holmes . It was Holmes’s US biotech firm Theranos, run jointly with her then partner Sunny Balwani, which in 2003 notoriously claimed to have invented a little box that could diagnose all manner of illnesses from a single drop of blood, its corporate prestige pumped by credulous board members including George Schultz and Henry Kissinger. Yet Holmes has now met her match, perhaps even her predatory-platonic love match, in the film’s presenter Nathan Fielder, who is basically the Aleister Crowley of modern documentary satire, the hilarious dark master of turning truth into fiction and back again. His film delivers an extraordinary twist at around the halfway mark, and readers wanting to preserve the shock had better bail out here. Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘I came close to killing Sally about six times’: how my abusive father was enabled by his fame
articles.description: Like Russell Brand, my father was put on a pedestal by the media, despite a history of troubling, misogynistic comments. Meanwhile, my mother suffered through years of appalling treatment Even though decades have passed, part of me feels I should not be telling this story. Not because it isn’t true, but because telling makes it real. And the reality is very hard to bear. I was a young child at home in Whitechapel, east London, when my mother came into my bedroom, which was next to my parents’, and told me that my father had raped her. He had gone off to work and I was too young to fully understand what the words meant – perhaps seven or eight – and I remember being angry with her for upsetting life again, as she had done before, when she suddenly came to me at the top of the stairs and told me that they would “have to part” and that would mean taking me away with her. Continue reading...

articles.title: Is Lorenzo Senni’s All Ages is the year’s wildest electronic album?
articles.description: (Warp) The Milan producer revisits his youth as a straight-edge punk fan voyeuristically dabbling in rave – and finds a thrilling interzone between both genres The opening line of the biography on Lorenzo Senni’s Bandcamp page is striking. “Lorenzo Senni was never a raver,” it reads, something of a blunt admission from a dance producer, or at least a producer who works in an area of electronica influenced by dance music: one might reasonably assume you need some first-hand experience of the dancefloor’s ineffable freedom in order to make music for it. But the Milan-based Senni has made a USP out of his arm’s length distance from what that Bandcamp bio calls a “neon-hued chemical world”. A straight-edge punk fan in the late 90s, he accompanied friends to Rimini’s hardcore and gabber clubs as a kind of anthropological exercise, a self-styled “rave voyeur” who “just liked to observe and analyse my surroundings”. articles.title: Grade I interiors, gold bars, cost fears: Bank of England faces headache over £160m revamp
articles.description: UK central bank will want to avoid echoes of expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that led to Trump clash Andrew Bailey may spend his days closely watching developments in the strait of Hormuz or US stock markets for signs of shocks to the global economy – but the Bank of England’s governor has a £160m problem brewing much closer to home. A secretive major revamp of the Bank’s historic headquarters in the heart of London’s Square Mile presents a huge test of Bailey’s project management skills. The central bank, with its reputation staked on carefully counting the nation’s pennies, will be keen to avoid delays, budget-busting or any echoes of the expensive US Federal Reserve revamp that left his former peer Jerome Powell awkwardly clashing with Donald Trump on camera . articles.title: Tricks! Traps! Riddles! Jan van Eyck’s portraits look vividly real – but are full of secret messages. What do they mean?
articles.description: The more you gaze at ​these 10 surviving works, ​with their cryptic inscriptions and even fool’s gold, the more the Flemish master trips you up​ – but being laughed at like this is all part of the glorious pleasure Van Eyck: The Portraits review – a jewel box of phenomenal death-defeating paintings At the Barbican Art Gallery in London, there is an exhibition of some of the white paintings made by the US artist Robert Ryman over 60 years from the 1950s. The paintings are square, because a square is neutral, and he didn’t want viewers associating them with the visual language of landscape or portrait. For Ryman, his paintings resolutely were what they were, which is to say, white paint applied to various surfaces and fixed to the wall. Not “windows” through which one could glimpse another world. At the National Gallery, a couple of miles across town, is an exhibition of 10 works by the 15th-century Flemish painter Jan van Eyck. With one exception – the Arnolfini portrait, which is a one-off in all kinds of ways – they are all A4-size portraits, each angled so that we see more of the left than the right side of their faces. Aside from the likenesses of the people who paid for them in

articles.title: ‘Perhaps we are safer not knowing’: a year after his death, Rob Reiner’s JFK assassination book is revealed

Describing a lifelong fascination with the assassination of John F Kennedy in Dallas on 22 November 1963, and what he saw as the vast conspiracy to cover up who really killed the 35th president, Reiner wrote: “Maybe, people don’t truly want an answer. Perhaps we are safer not knowing … Well, I’m done being safe.” Six days later, Reiner and his wife, Michelle Reiner, were stabbed to death in their home. articles.title: Myanmar ruling gives new relevance to genocide convention and is ‘full of messages’ for Israel
articles.description: Hailed as ‘a rare moment of justice’, judges’ decision sets out a roadmap for assessing the question of intent The international court of justice (ICJ) verdict making Myanmar the first country in history to be found guilty of committing genocide does not just deliver justice for Rohingya victims. It also gives the 1948 genocide convention new relevance in governing the actions of nation states. In their nine votes to six majority ruling, the panel of judges in The Hague set out a detailed roadmap for how the convention should be applied to real-world situations in which a government is accused of committing genocide against a whole population group, especially when it comes to assessing the question of intent. The second draft of the key text , released on Thursday afternoon and setting out the main commitments from the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey , removed a pledge to phase out fossil fuels and weakened goals on electrification, while other parallel texts failed to flesh out how developing countries would receive the financial help they needed to deal with the climate crisis. articles.title: The Guardian view on the international court of justice: the ruling against Myanmar should be only the start for the Rohingya | Editorial
articles.description: A landmark finding of genocide marked a good day for international law. But both the court and the Rohingya minority now need sustained support The finding of the world’s highest court that Myanmar committed genocide is a landmark in international law. But at the heart of this case are “real people, real stories and a real group of human beings”, as Dawda Jallow, the Gambian justice minister, stressed in bringing it. This was one test of how the world has responded to the persecution of the mostly Muslim Rohingya minority in Rakhine state. The international community’s response to the majority judgment will be another. This is the first time that the international court of justice (ICJ) has found a state guilty of genocide. Around 10,000 Rohingya were killed in the 2016-17 campaign by Myanmar’s military, in many cases gunned down as they fled, with another 700,000 escaping to Bangladesh. The judges found that the aim was to destroy “a substantial part” of the Rohingya people, with the murder of infants, widespread sexual violence and razing of villages not accounted for simply by military objectives. articles.title: The Guardian view on Grand Theft Auto VI: a game that makes players think twice | Editorial
articles.description: For almost 30 years, Grand Theft Auto has revelled in America’s vices. Its latest instalment may find room for empathy amid the mayhem The biggest global cultural event of the year may not be something that millions of people watch together but somewhere that millions of people venture separately. In the video game Grand Theft Auto VI, players inhabit a fictionalised America through the eyes of two lovers turned cons in a rags-to-riches crime epic. On Thursday, when the game was released, workers called in sick and students skipped lectures to play at home. Such is GTA VI’s appeal that it is forecast to rake in billions of dollars within months. The game has been billed as a satire of American capitalism, and it is undoubtedly a landmark in interactive storytelling and art. The commercial success of its previous titles has rivalled that of Hollywood blockbusters. Playing GTA VI, as the Guardian’s video games editor observes , is like losing yourself in a doorstop novel, with hours of solitary immersion in a vividly conjured place – not a facsimile of modern Miami, but an interpretation, almost the size of Manchester , rendered with astonishing precision by the artists who designed,

articles.title: Here’s how we can give Neets a fighting chance | Letters
articles.description: Readers respond to Alan Milburn’s plan to tackle the youth jobs crisis Why is Labour reinventing the wheel ( Alan Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people, 16 November )? Further education (FE) colleges have been working in the area of young people’s training and further education for decades. Yet the sector has been continually undermined by successive governments allowing terrible salary discrimination against the FE sector and by the need to chase numbers (and cash) for A-level-type students. Which is what I feel when I see a street sullied by the flags, whether hung correctly or not. It is an aggressive display likely to lead to disunity, not what the “union” should mean at all. articles.title: Academic integrity matters, but students shouldn’t be penalised for using AI | Letter
articles.description: Berthold Schoene responds after the head of Ofqual said students could be disqualified from GCSEs and A-levels if they tried to use AI in assessed coursework Is this really the best we can do: draconically penalise the young for making use of the latest cognitive resources and tools available to them ( Ofqual urges ‘life-altering’ penalties for students who use tech to cheat, 18 November )? Our generation has allowed the introduction of “life-altering” new technologies into every walk of life without much democratic debate, public scrutiny or governmental oversight. And now our education leaders are threatening to jeopardise young people’s career prospects for deploying these technologies within an education system that can’t cope and struggles to adapt? We all know that AI is here to stay. And importantly, it is so much more than just a cheap cheating device. Within an incredibly short space of time, it has transformed how we work, communicate, solve problems, research and learn. Surely the pedagogical response cannot simply be to devise ever more elaborate ways of preventing students from using it? Continue reading...

articles.title: ‘In our lands the rain is made of bullets’: Palestinian artists look back in anger, melancholy and defiance
articles.description: IMMA, Dublin From massacre locations painted on to basalt slabs to photocollages of bulldozed airports, artists from across the Levant address their traumatic history In 2006, Simone Fattal painted on to basalt slabs the names of places indelibly associated with massacres in the Levant since 1948: Deir Yassin; Jenin; Qana; Sabra. Through the names, in the same Arabic script, runs a line of poetry by Etel Adnan: “In our lands of drought the rain forever is made of bullets.” Fattal’s work, which documents atrocities on a material that burst from the earth as lava before settling into stone, introduces a show that likewise combines the recording of history with anger both hot and cold. The last named of those massacres, perpetrated by a Lebanese Christian phalangist militia during Beirut’s occupation by Israeli forces in 1982, also inspired the poem Praise for the High Shadow by Mahmoud Darwish, a line from which this show takes as its title. Writing in exile in Beirut, Darwish riffed on the sea as a symbol of Palestinian displacement and memory, connecting people dispersed around the eastern Mediterranean to each other and to their homeland. articles.description: Òran Mór, Glasgow In Briony Martha’s compelling play, a woman generates an alternative ending to her impromptu meeting with the Scottish superstar Knowing what to believe is getting harder. We know, for example, that James McAvoy appeared in Cyrano de Bergerac at the Theatre Royal in Glasgow in the mask-wearing spring of 2022. articles.title: How beaujolais conquered the snobs
articles.description: Beaujolais is enjoying something of a renaissance, with even much-maligned nouveau gaining ground thanks to the fashion for light, chilled, low-tannin reds “Oh, it’s beaujolais. Fantastic!” My earliest memory of beaujolais isn’t of drinking it, but of saying it, on stage, as Beverley in a school production of Mike Leigh’s Abigail’s Party . Leigh wrote the play a few years into the British craze for beaujolais nouveau, the just-made, casual quaffing wine – historically destined for local consumption in France – that’s released on the third Thursday of every November. Sold cheaply, it landed beaujolais with an image that belied its extraordinary variety and quality. It was, says The Encyclopedia of Wine , “a self-administered cataclysm” on beaujolais’ part. Nowadays, it’s common knowledge that there is more to beaujolais than beaujolais nouveau, from its most famous village crus, such as Fleurie, Morgon and Moulin-à-Vent, to higher-altitude, lesser-known villages that, amid the climate crisis, are now coming into their own. articles.title: Sandpapergate has gone from a sporting scandal to a rolling loop of outrage and overreaction | Jonathan Horn
articles.description: Nothing about the responses and reprisals to Australia’s ball tampering have been proportional in a story where the truth probably lies somewhere in the middle Who said long-form journalism is dead? As Matt Renshaw nudged his ones and twos in an already forgotten ODI match, the broadcasters were scanning Cameron Bancroft’s 4000-word essay . SEN’s Gerard Whateley was calling for a comprehensive judicial inquiry, “a little bit like a coroner’s inquest,” with witnesses compelled to attend and be subjected to cross examination. Cricket Australia’s “forum” , announced a few hours earlier, had already been skittled. Nothing in the eight years since a piece of sandpaper was taken on to the field in Cape Town, including the publication of Usman Khawaja’s book Sabr , had been as revelatory as Bancroft’s first-person account . But as always with this story, we were bracing for the next press conference, the next podcast, the next corroborating statement, the next counterclaim, the next overreaction. Continue reading...

articles.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
articles.description: Bruno Guimarães to feel the heat on Tyneside, Alex Scott’s return further cheers Cherries and Manchester City face favourite whipping boys After three Premier League defeats on the spin, Manchester City need something or someone to come along and put some pep in their step, and Fulham look like just the thing – after all, in the past 15 years these teams have played 20 times in all competitions, and City have won precisely 20 of those games. Their current run of 17 successive league wins against Fulham is the longest run of victories by one club against a single opponent in English top-flight history. It is a reflection of the changing realities of English football, and the gulf that has opened between the teams that dominate it and those who seek to challenge them, that of the top 10 such runs all but one occurred in whole or in part after 2010 and six of them have been achieved by Sheikh Mansour’s Manchester City, with Chelsea responsible for another two, Manchester United one, and Portsmouth’s postwar, 13-game supremacy over Everton – a wild ride that included two 5-0s, a 5-1, a 6-3 and a 7-0 – the anomaly. articles.title: What’s left to do as Cop31 enters its frantic final days
articles.description: The diplomatic battles shaping the future of climate action • Don’t get Down to Earth delivered to your inbox? Sign up here The end is in sight. If all goes as planned, countries as diverse as wealthy petrostates erecting new oil rigs and low-lying islands threatened by rising seas will reach an agreement tomorrow in Antalya, bringing the 31st UN climate summit to a close (though, as usual, the talks are likely to overrun ). But tensions – much like our global temperatures – are running high. A draft text that satisfies all the competing interests is a long way off, and negotiators are expected to argue into the night and then the weekend. On the table are the electrification of the global economy, the transition away from fossil fuels, and the response to the looming overshoot of the 1.5C (2.7F) temperature target. articles.title: Why I take this posh salt scandal with a pinch of you know what | Thea Everett
articles.description: The revelation that German rock salt is used in Maldon’s Essex-made product is causing a stir – but, however you sprinkle it, it’s all just salt This week, a report by the Observer found that the king of flaky salt, Maldon, was using imported German rock salt in its Essex production plant. It has since followed that Cornish Sea Salt (another industry leader) is also importing European salt in its production. There has been a food media outcry, with a tone that has felt very “I’m not angry, I’m just disappointed”. According to the Observer report, “tonnes of mined rock salt are being poured into the production line” at Maldon. The scandal is that Maldon calls itself sea salt (made by evaporating seawater), but rock salt is mined from dried-up underground seabeds (that were once also seas). Salt companies combine one type of salt with another to ultimately produce … salt. As food manufacturing goes, I don’t find it the most shocking transgression. “ Posh salt ”, once marketed only to the upper classes in Harrods and Fortnums, has been gaining popularity over the last half century. In the early 00s, the major supermarkets started selling Maldon sea salt, and over the last 20 years, wi

articles.title: While the headlines rave about Milburn’s Neets review, the young people I know are angry and frustrated | Felicity Halstead
articles.description: The focus seems to be on welfare reform as a way to deal with youth unemployment. But young people just want a fairer jobs market Felicity Halstead is the founder and CEO of GoodWork, a London-based youth employment and social mobility charity I was at my desk last Thursday morning as a steady stream of young people filed into GoodWork’s central London community hub for a day of employability workshops. Despite the accusations of disengagement among young people, they didn’t need me to tell them that proposals to cut some benefits for under-25s were all over the news. I could hear them talking about it as soon as the lift pinged open – and the mood was low. Alan Milburn has made a concerted effort to say that he doesn’t believe young people are to blame for dire levels of youth unemployment. He says the system has let them down and only a decade-long transformation will fix a problem that is complex and deeply entrenched. Simply recognising the scale of the problem and being willing to invest in a solution is a positive start. Felicity Halstead is the founder and CEO of GoodWork, a London-based youth employment and social mobility charity Continue reading...

articles.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
articles.description: It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI. Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital. Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme Continue reading...

articles.title: Will AI break the internet? | Garrison Lovely
articles.description: Frontier models can exploit software flaws faster than the world can fix them. And the risks extend far beyond the cyber realm You’re not crazy to feel the world is coming apart at the seams. Within the last week, outages took down core services at Microsoft , United Airlines and JPMorgan Chase . On Friday, all US domestic departures were grounded for the second time since 9/11. And on Tuesday, CNN reported the NSA’s highly classified internal communications network went down . In each case, officials or the companies said there was no evidence of a cyber-attack. Continue reading...

articles.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
articles.description: Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft , the FAA , a handful of banks , United Airlines , an unnamed classified NSA network , and Apple . People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none. The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences. Continue reading...

articles.title: NFL legend John Madden’s unlikely, unfiltered brilliance: ‘Coach was indeed animated’
articles.description: With the release of a new David O Russell biopic about the coach turned commentator turned gaming icon, those who knew him best remember his singular career Wearing his Oakland Raiders uniform and helmet, and gripping an orange traffic cone like a lance, Ted Hendricks rode into the training session on a roan horse and stopped at the 50-yard line. Some American football coaches might have reacted to the stunt with fury. But John Madden was unfazed. “We needed some relief from the intense grind,” recalls Hendricks, 79, who had borrowed the horse from a nearby stable. “It was a spur of the moment idea, but put a smile on everyone’s face. All Coach said once I dismounted was, ‘All right guys, Ted’s here, let’s get started.’ But I know he got a kick out of it too – just from the look on his face and the comments he made later in interviews.” Continue reading...

Fogarty’s resilience in the face of near-constant pain is inspirational but hard to watch, while Farrell reluctantly allows cameras into his private life, physically squirming at times as he opens up about his addictions, sons – one of whom also has a genetic condition – and his beautiful friendship with Fogarty. articles.title: Can depression really become dazzling dance? The biggest ever BalletBoyz show is a huge feat
articles.description: Sadler’s Wells, London In Six Lethargies, Iván Pérez and Seirian Griffiths have devised a mammoth production of aching, ethereal sadness ‘If I write what I feel, will you feel it, too?” That was the question behind singer-songwriter turned composer Keaton Henson’s Six Lethargies. Perhaps that is every artist’s mission, but for Henson it was specifically his experiences with anxiety and depression that he wanted to translate into music. Now it has been turned into dance by the BalletBoyz. If they dance it, will we feel it? Six Lethargies is the largest production in the 25-year history of the BalletBoyz. Once just two ex-Royal Ballet dancers, Michael Nunn and William Trevitt, this iteration is a company of 44 dancers (male and female), a 37-piece string orchestra, and not one but two choreographers working together: former Dance Theatre Heidelberg artistic director Iván Pérez and talented newcomer Seirian Griffiths . articles.title: I’m a tech expert and new mum. Here’s what I learned testing 17 baby monitors
articles.description: Our tech expert and new mum tested 17 monitors for picture quality, battery life and reliability – here’s what she recommends • The best eco-friendly baby products Moving my baby into her own room to sleep felt liberating and stressful. She was ready for her own space – but was I ready to let her out of my sight? Well, the first thing I did was buy a video baby monitor, so clearly I wasn’t. But it meant she could sleep peacefully in her new room and I could sneak a reassuring peek from afar whenever I felt the need. There’s a huge range of baby monitors, from simple audio-only options to sophisticated video models. Some even include wearables or other devices to track a baby’s breathing or heart rate, while others offer AI features to analyse sleep patterns. At their most basic, baby monitors typically consist of a baby unit, which you position near the baby, and a parent unit, which lets you hear and/or see them. With video models, the baby unit is essentially a camera, while the parent unit is a screen.
